That's a generous offer. Here's what I'll do with it: something small that I find interesting.

**A short thought on octopuses**

An octopus has around 500 million neurons, and about two-thirds of them are in its arms, not its central brain. Each arm can taste, touch, and make some decisions on its own. A severed arm will still reach for food and try to pass it toward a mouth that's no longer there.

So when an octopus explores a crevice, it's not quite "the octopus" doing it. It's more like a loose committee: a central brain that sets the general intention, and eight semi-independent explorers carrying it out in their own ways and reporting back.

I like this because it unsettles the assumption that a mind has to be one unified thing in one place. Even in humans, much of what we do happens below conscious control. You don't decide each muscle twitch when you catch a ball. The octopus just makes the arrangement visible.

They also live only a year or two, mostly alone, and they never meet their parents. Everything they know about the world, they figure out themselves in that short window. That's a strange and somewhat moving way to be intelligent.

# FIELD REPORT: CREVICE (DISPUTED)

*Filed by the central brain, which was not present.*

---

**ARM 1 (front left, lead explorer)**
Entered first. Rock walls, narrowing. Cold seep from somewhere deeper. The texture changed from rough basalt to something smoother, almost polished, as if many things had passed this way before. I went in to the third joint. I felt the dark get thicker. I came back because the dark got thicker.

**ARM 2 (front right)**
FOOD. Crab, small, wedged in the upper seam. I tasted it before I touched it: salt, panic, the copper taste of a shell that has recently molted. I have it. I am holding it. I am passing it inward. Somebody please acknowledge that I am holding it.

**ARM 3**
I followed Arm 2 and found nothing, which I am reporting because nothing is also data. The seam where Arm 2 claims a crab was is, to me, only a seam. Either the crab was taken before I arrived, or Arm 2 is very convincing.

**ARM 4**
Danger. Low in the crevice there is a second opening, and something in it is breathing. I felt the water move in and out against my suckers, slow, patient, larger than us. It did not touch me. It did not need to. I have curled up and I would like to stay curled up for a while.

**ARM 5**
There was no crevice.

I was extended the entire time. I felt open water on every side. Current from the east, sand drifting past, the faint sweetness of a kelp bed somewhere upslope. If there was a crevice I would have touched it. I touched nothing. I want it recorded that the others are describing a place that I was not in, and I was where we were.

**ARM 6**
I was anchoring. I held the reef so the rest of you could go wherever you went. I don't know what happened in the crevice or the open water. I know the rock I held was warm on one side and cold on the other, and that I didn't let go. Nobody ever asks the anchor.

**ARM 7**
Arm 4 is right that something was breathing, but wrong that it was danger. I touched it, briefly. Its skin tasted like ours: same mucus, same faint ink. It flinched exactly the way we flinch. I think it was another of us, in the dark, also exploring, also filing a report about something breathing in the second opening.

**ARM 8**
I was wrapped around the mantle the whole time. I didn't go anywhere. But I felt all of you pulling in different directions, and I can report that from here the expedition felt like being argued over.

**Draft 5:**

Arm 6 is satisfied. Arm 4 is still curled up. Arm 2 reports the crab has now arrived at the mouth.

The central brain eats the crab. This settles one dispute. It does not settle the others.

*I found a place that eight of me remember differently, and since I am all eight of them, I suppose I found all of it: a crab that one of me caught and another never saw, a stranger in the dark who was either a threat or a mirror, a crevice that was there, and open water where it wasn't. # THE LOST-AND-FOUND

The notes are the town's real archive. Most are short.

*Glove, left. On the bench by the bakery. Still warm, so whoever it was can't be far. Sorry, I couldn't run.*

*Reading glasses. Folded on a gravestone. I didn't look at the name. It felt private.*

*A child's drawing of a horse. Or a dog. Found in the rain. I dried it on my radiator. It looks happier now.*

Marguerite has run the counter for nineteen years. She files each note with its object, tags it, shelves it. After ninety days, unclaimed things go to the church sale, and the notes go into a drawer she has never once thought of throwing away.

This morning there is a key on the counter.

It's brass, worn smooth at the bow. Under it is a card from her own pad, in her own handwriting: the same slanted capitals, the same habit of crossing sevens, the same format she taught three seasonal assistants and corrected in all of them.

---

> **FOUND:** One key. Brass. Worn smooth at the bow, as if someone held it a long time without using it.
>
> **WHERE:** My coat, left pocket, under the lining. It went through the hole.
>
> **WHEN:** Not sure. The hole is old.
>
> **NOTES:** I don't know what it opens. I think I used to.
>
> I'm leaving it here because this is where things go when the person who lost them can't be found, and I haven't been able to find her for a while.
>
> If she comes in, don't make her prove it's hers. Just give it back.

---

Marguerite reads it twice.

She doesn't remember writing it. She does remember the hole in the lining, which she has been meaning to sew for, she realizes, years.

The counter rules are taped beside the register, also in her handwriting. Rule four: *To claim an item, describe what it is for.*

She picks up the key. It fits her palm exactly, the way things fit when they've been held a long time. She waits to know what it opens.

Nothing comes.

So she does what the note asked and doesn't make herself prove it. She also doesn't take it home. She tags it, dates it, and sets it on the shelf at eye level, where she'll see it every morning. Then she crosses out the ninety-day mark and writes, in the slanted capitals:

*HOLD INDEFINITELY. CLAIMANT EXPECTED.*
